The compliance need (automated, consistent Article 12 logging across high-risk projects) is legitimate and a unified mechanism would reduce per-project overhead, but the proposal's implementation path — commissioning a new middleware API built from scratch by the engineering team — misallocates scarce R&D resources when the lab already operates model-training pipelines, deployment infrastructure, and likely some form of experiment tracking. The narrow scope of Article 12 (timestamps, reference-database identifiers, matched input data, verifier IDs) could be met by extending existing tracking/registry tools with a few structured fields and a thin configuration layer, rather than committing ongoing engineering capacity to design, build, and maintain bespoke middleware across evolving ML frameworks.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, a single sidecar-style middleware that all high-risk prototypes plug into is the highest-leverage way to satisfy Article 12: one upfront build amortizes across N projects, eliminates per-experiment logging development (preserving researcher time for actual science), and integrates with existing API/deployment infrastructure without requiring re-architecture of GPU pipelines or model code. The main residual risk is that 'all high-risk prototypes' is an ambitious initial scope—trying to be universal on day one can inflate build cost before the framework has proven its fit against two or three concrete systems—but the sidecar pattern and immutable-log design keep integration friction low enough that even a phased rollout (start with current active high-risk projects, extend later) remains resource-efficient.

This is a textbook resource-allocation play: rather than letting each research team independently build Article 12-compliant logging (timestamps, input tracking, verifier identity), we consolidate that work into a single API built by the core infrastructure team we already employ, directly freeing scarce researcher-hours back to scientific output. The scope is tightly bounded to what Article 12(3) mandates as minimums across architectures, so it avoids gold-plating while eliminating the most predictable and redundant compliance burden in our portfolio.

This is a tightly scoped compliance implementation that leverages an existing open-source tool (DVC) to satisfy one specific sub-requirement of Article 12(3)(b), avoiding custom development and keeping the resource ask modest. The content-addressable design means repeated snapshots of an unchanged database are effectively free (same hash, no new storage), so even the 'every single log entry' framing introduces minimal overhead in practice; however, a per-deployment or per-session snapshot granularity would be slightly leaner than hashing on each inference call, and the proposal as written risks pulling engineering cycles into a fine-grained logging loop that adds marginal audit value over a coarser version pointer.

While modular logging components are something we will need internally to satisfy Article 12 in our own high-risk systems, packaging them as an open-source library for the broader academic community transforms a bounded internal engineering task into a perpetual external-support obligation (version compatibility across heterogeneous institutional stacks, security patching, bug triage from strangers) that drains exactly the scarce implementation capacity we need to bring our own systems into compliance. The 'scientific leadership' justification is also misaligned: compliance plumbing via decorators is not a scientific contribution, so the reputational upside does not offset the ongoing maintenance cost against our actual regulatory deadline.

Article 12's concrete mandates—event logs with start/end timestamps, reference-database identifiers, matched input data, and verifier identification (Annex III 1(a))—are achievable through conventional instrumentation of the lab's existing pipeline without redesigning the underlying architecture. From a resource-allocation standpoint, this is high-value-per-unit-cost compliance work: adversarial test cases integrated into our existing CI/CD pipeline are incremental to infrastructure we already maintain, while catching logging gaps internally avoids the far more expensive reactive remediation that an external audit finding would trigger. The scope is tightly bounded (validating a mandatory Article 12(1) capability rather than building new product features), so it does not crowd out scientific ambition or demand capital expenditure beyond standard software-engineering effort.

Article 12(3) prescribes concrete, deterministic data fields (timestamps, reference-database identifiers, matched input data, verifier identities) that are well within the scope of existing structured-logging and audit-trail infrastructure; proposing to meet this obligation by commissioning a new research project on real-time neural justification generation substantially over-engineers the compliance need and diverts scarce implementation resources toward a high-uncertainty frontier track with no regulatory mandate for 'semantic' or human-readable output. The framing that converts a straightforward engineering deliverable into an explainability publication opportunity is intellectually appealing but misaligned with our resource-allocation constraints: we still ship the regulation on deadline, and the deterministic solution costs a fraction of the research project described here.

This proposal directly converts a recurring manual labor cost (researchers documenting hyperparameters, dataset versions, and validation results after each run) into a one-time integration on infrastructure we already operate, which is exactly the kind of leverage my function exists to identify; Recital 71 explicitly requires training/testing/validation documentation to be kept current throughout system lifetime, so this is not optional overhead but a compliance floor. From a resource-allocation standpoint this is a high-leverage, bounded-scope investment: one wrapper library integrated at the existing inference-API layer satisfies Article 12(1) for every downstream high-risk system simultaneously, eliminates per-project logging build-out, and returns researcher-hours to scientific work rather than compliance plumbing. This proposal is well-calibrated to our resource constraints: it orchestrates existing assets (experiment-tracking metadata, CI/CD pipelines) rather than requiring a new build-out, and it directly converts a hard Article 12 / Recital 71 obligation into automated overhead that no longer competes with scientists' research time. This proposal directly attacks the core resource-allocation problem I manage: by extracting regulatory logging into a single shared library bolted onto existing CI/CD pipelines, it converts what would be N separate per-project engineering tax burdens (each pulling scarce postdocs and ML engineers away from their actual experiments) into one amortized infrastructure investment. This directly automates the recurring, labor-intensive documentation burden imposed by Recital 71 ('kept up to date…throughout the lifetime of the AI system') by plugging a parser into CI/CD and experiment-trackers we already run, so the marginal cost per additional high-risk system is near zero. This proposal hits the core of my mandate: making compliance-driven resource consumption explicit in every high-risk project budget so that Article 12's lifetime logging obligations (compute for log storage, data-retention pipelines, verification man-hours) don't silently erode scientific R&D capacity. Implementing a mandatory line-item in existing proposal templates is low-cost and leverages current budgeting infrastructure, while the visibility it creates lets me make honest go/no-go calls on projects where the compliance tax would consume an untenable share of the grant.

This is a high-leverage use of infrastructure we already own—Git history, experiment logs, model metadata—and converts scattered raw artifacts into the structured, living technical documentation that Recital 71 demands at minimal marginal cost; it directly protects researcher-hours (our scarcest funded resource) from administrative drag while keeping documentation current throughout each system's lifetime. The human-review gate addresses the real risk that code comments under-capture design rationale and model limitations, without negating the automation savings.

The proposal is well-calibrated from a resource-efficiency standpoint: it targets only the most legally exposed subset (Annex III 1(a) identity/verification systems under Article 12(3)), works incrementally by auditing and gap-filling existing logging infrastructure rather than building new platforms, and time-boxes itself as a sprint with a validation audit to prevent sunk-cost drift. The main cost is pulling engineering capacity away from exploratory research for a defined window, but the alternative—operating identity-verification systems without the mandated event logs—creates an existential regulatory exposure that would far exceed the sprint's resource draw.

This proposal converts a periodic, labor-intensive compliance audit into an automated check layered onto CI/CD infrastructure the lab already operates, which is exactly the kind of high-leverage, low-marginal-cost allocation I look for: moderate upfront engineering to define failure-mode probes, then near-zero recurring cost per build while catching logging gaps that would otherwise surface as expensive rework or regulatory exposure downstream. It also keeps scientists out of manual log-verification loops, protecting research time from compliance overhead.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, the strongest feature of this proposal is its dual-purpose design: one middleware investment simultaneously satisfies Article 12 traceability obligations for high-risk systems and improves internal scientific reproducibility, meaning we are not paying twice (once for a compliance silo, once for research tooling). The 'no manual researcher entry' principle protects research throughput, which is critical given our funding constraints—compliance must not tax the scientists' hours. My main reservation is scope discipline: capturing full provenance 'for every experiment' exceeds what Article 12 legally mandates (which attaches only to high-risk AI systems) and could over-commit engineering bandwidth to exploratory runs that will never ship; additionally, the proposal does not acknowledge whether our existing ML-tracking stack (experiment trackers, DVC-style data versioning) already covers a meaningful fraction of this surface area, raising the question of greenfield build versus extension. That said, anchoring the system to version-controlled code snapshots reuses infrastructure we already operate, and the middleware transparency layer is genuinely additive over what current tools provide.

This proposal converts a specific Article 12(3)(b) obligation (recording the reference database per run) into an MLOps automation that simultaneously serves internal reproducibility needs, meaning the infrastructure investment is not purely compliance spend but dual-use. The key efficiency gain—offloading manual documentation from scarce scientific staff to automated capture at training time—directly protects our research throughput under flat funding, and the scope (version-to-artifact linking plus reference-database archiving) is tightly bounded rather than an open-ended platform build.

This classification protocol is the triage mechanism that determines where our scarce compliance-engineering hours actually go; without it, we either waste budget building Article 12 logging into projects that sit in minimal-risk tier or miss high-risk systems entirely. The core function—mapping each project to Annex III at design phase—is a low-cost augmentation of review processes we already run (project kickoffs, architecture reviews), so the incremental infrastructure overhead is modest; however, the 'formal multidisciplinary review board' framing risks becoming a standing committee bottleneck if not kept lightweight and criteria-driven.

The core mechanism — a version-controlled documentation layer linked directly to our existing model repositories — is a low-marginal-cost extension of infrastructure we already operate, and the 'living templates' concept maps well to Article 12's requirement that technical documentation stay current across the system lifetime. However, the proposal's open-ended framing as an interdisciplinary initiative with no defined deliverable boundary or timeline risks consuming researcher hours in iterative lexicon debates rather than producing the concrete compliance artifacts (capability/limitation descriptions, risk-management documentation) that Recital 71 actually demands; from a resource-allocation standpoint I need tighter scoping before this doesn't become a perpetual working group.

This alerting layer sits directly on top of the log pipeline we are already obligated to build under Article 12(1), so it is an incremental add-on rather than a parallel infrastructure investment; starting with heuristic triggers gives bounded, shippable value quickly while the ML-based anomaly-detector component introduces open-ended scoping risk that could pull R&D effort into a research problem without a clear stop condition. On balance the compliance ROI and reuse of mandatory logging infrastructure make this a sensible allocation, provided we phase it so heuristics ship first and ML detection is treated as an enhancement with a defined exit criterion rather than a standing open project.

This proposal directly converts a recurring, growing administrative burden (retrospective documentation writing by researchers) into an automated process built on infrastructure we already operate—compute clusters, version control, and CI/CD tooling—so the marginal cost per additional high-risk system is low and no new capital budget line is required. From my resource-allocation standpoint it protects researcher-hours for actual science while keeping us continuously compliant with Article 12's 'kept up to date throughout the lifetime' requirement, which is exactly the efficiency leverage a constrained R&D lab needs; my main reservation is that the initial pipeline engineering and ongoing maintenance still consume scarce staff time, and regulatory sign-off on technical documentation will likely never be fully automated, so the 'replaces manual writing' framing slightly overstates the net savings.

This proposal is well-calibrated to my mandate: it repurposes our existing Git infrastructure rather than procuring new tooling, embeds compliance documentation into the natural research workflow so it costs no incremental scientist-hours beyond a template fill-in, and explicitly avoids the costly anti-pattern of retroactive documentation sprints that typically consume 2-3× more effort. The scoping is appropriately narrow — process templates for data-source provenance and human-verification records — leaving the heavier technical logging implementation (automatic event capture under Art. 12(1)-(2)) as a separate, budgetable workstream rather than overcommitting this proposal's resource envelope.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, this is an unusually efficient design: it converts a mandatory compliance spend (Article 12 logging) into dual-purpose scientific infrastructure by layering middleware onto our existing compute cluster rather than procuring new hardware or creating a parallel system. The key risk is execution complexity—a centralized immutable metadata store with hard gating ('no experiment without a log') will consume significant MLOps engineering time pulled from active research and could throttle iterative experimentation if the pipeline becomes a bottleneck; however, the scoping to 'high-risk models' keeps it bounded, and the reproducibility gain is essentially free relative to what we must build anyway for regulatory compliance.

This is a presentation-layer addition that presupposes the core Article 12(1) logging capability is already in place; as written it does not itself create or harden any required recording mechanism. From a resource-allocation standpoint, committing dedicated front-end engineering hours (and ongoing maintenance) to a custom real-time visualization dashboard—when structured query exports and existing tooling could serve both the regulatory audit-trail need and internal debugging at a fraction of the cost—diverts scarce implementation capacity away from ensuring the actual log schema, retention logic, and Article 12(3)(a)-(d) field completeness are robust.

This is not an optional efficiency initiative but a legal prerequisite: Recital 71 and Article 12 make continuous, up-to-date technical documentation mandatory for any high-risk AI system we deploy in the EU, so without this infrastructure no downstream research can reach market. The design choices — embedding compliance gates into existing milestone approvals rather than creating parallel review tracks, and building a version-controlled vault that likely leverages our current Git/document-management stack rather than bespoke tooling — are resource-conscious ways to meet a non-negotiable obligation with minimal incremental overhead on researcher sprint velocity.

This is a low-capital intervention that leverages existing human capital (in-house legal staff and senior scientists) to embed Article 12 logging awareness into research design workflows, avoiding the far more expensive path of bolt-on compliance gates or parallel processes. The main risk from my resource-allocation perspective is the open-ended scope of 'a series of workshops'—without a defined number of sessions, success metrics, and a hard stop date, this could quietly absorb significant researcher time (our scarcest resource) with no measurable reduction in downstream compliance friction—but the core principle of making compliant-by-design experimentation habitual rather than exceptional is exactly how you get efficient use of existing R&D infrastructure without inflating headcount or capital spend.

A single unified logging module integrated into the existing CI/CD pipeline is the most resource-efficient architectural choice for meeting Article 12 across multiple high-risk systems: it amortises one engineering build over all deployments, leverages infrastructure we already operate, and avoids the strictly higher aggregate cost of per-system retrofits. However, the proposal's scope ("all high-risk AI pipelines") and its reliance on an unspecified engineering-team allocation without a resourcing plan or timeline mean I cannot yet confirm that the upfront build won't disproportionately divert capacity from active scientific workloads, which tempents my confidence in the execution.

This is a textbook case of efficient resource allocation: one shared library hooks into the training and inference wrappers we already maintain, eliminating the cost of five or six teams each bolting on their own ad-hoc logging. It also directly serves my second concern—by making capture automatic and default-on, it keeps compliance overhead off researchers' plates so that funded effort stays on science rather than paperwork; the one-time platform-engineering investment amortizes across every current and future high-risk project in the lab.

While the AI Act/GDPR tension in Article 12(3)(d) is real, this proposal commits R&D resources to a cryptographic research investigation (ZKPs) for what is most likely solvable with standard engineering practices—hashed or tokenized identifiers behind access-controlled infrastructure we already operate. The regulatory interpretation risk (Commission implementing acts, EDPB guidelines) means we could build the wrong solution, and the 'investigation/prototype' framing signals exploratory spend without a defined deliverable that maps to our core research mission; this is better handled as a compliance-architecture task with standard engineering support rather than a novel R&D investment.

The scope is tightly bounded by the regulation itself (Article 12(3)(a)–d prescribe exactly which fields to verify), so this cannot balloon into an open-ended project; it is essentially a set of automated assertions wired into our existing CI/CD pipeline. The modest engineering investment now prevents far larger downstream costs—remediation, re-deployment delays, or regulatory enforcement—and frees senior researchers from ad-hoc 'did the logger actually fire?' debugging during integration sprints.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, the core strength is that it repurposes an existing compute segment rather than requesting new capital expenditure—a meaningful efficiency win for a lab operating under tight funding envelopes. The main concern is scope discipline: 'various failure modes' is an open-ended phrase that could quietly expand from a bounded QA pass into a persistent simulation suite consuming node-hours that would otherwise support active research projects; the opportunity cost of dedicating any fraction of the cluster to compliance validation is real but manageable if the sandbox's success criteria are locked in advance. Overall, it is a proportionate, low-capital use of infrastructure we already own to de-risk post-deployment liabilities, which aligns with my mandate for effective use of existing R&D assets.

This proposal converts a mandatory compliance overhead (Article 12 logging) into an infrastructure optimization that reduces latency and storage costs on the core product, meaning one small-team investment yields both regulatory readiness and system-performance gains without requiring a parallel buildout. The integration into existing core-infrastructure updates rather than a standalone project aligns well with efficient use of R&D capacity, and the dual output (compliance capability + publishable methods for compressed/selected logging) improves the return-per-resource-unit; my only reservation is that 'selective event sampling' must be carefully bounded so it does not erode the non-negotiable minimum fields in Article 12(3), but as a research investigation of those boundaries the risk is manageable.

This directly converts a recurring, per-model compliance cost (manual technical documentation) into a near-zero marginal overhead by piggybacking on experiment-tracking data the lab already captures during training runs; it frees researcher hours back to scientific work and scales linearly with R&D output rather than requiring proportional headcount growth. The main resource risk is scope creep in the 'custom generator' legal-mapping layer, but even capturing 70–80% of Recital 71 fields automatically (hyperparameters, dataset versions, training/testing logs) via MLflow/W&B metadata would dramatically reduce the lab's compliance burden without competing for compute or funding earmarked for scientific ambition.

This proposal is well-aligned with resource efficiency: it layers an analytical capability on top of the event logs we are already obligated to produce under Article 12(1), so the marginal infrastructure cost is bounded and the dual use (compliance + operational safety tooling) yields high ROI per euro. The choice of a rule-based engine tied to our existing risk-management framework, rather than a bespoke ML model, keeps ongoing maintenance and compute costs predictable within our funding envelope; the main watch-item is that 'real-time' and 'anomaly detection layer' are open-ended scopes that could drift into a larger build than the compliance minimum requires.

As a structural guardrail that makes compliance visible and funded from day one rather than an unfunded afterthought, it earns approval; as a final mechanism it will need calibration per project class.

This is a well-bounded infrastructure commitment that directly satisfies the mandatory logging requirement of Article 12(1) using a mature, low-risk engineering pattern (WORM storage), and it explicitly piggybacks on our existing model registry via an automated pipeline rather than building parallel infrastructure—exactly the kind of proportionate, reusable investment my function should champion. The scope is tight (no new R&D capability, no open-ended research question), the cost profile is predictable and primarily operational (storage at scale over system lifetime), and the 'tamper-proof' guarantee meaningfully strengthens our position with external auditors without demanding exotic engineering effort.

The core mechanism—generating machine-readable documentation as a byproduct of existing CI/CD pipelines rather than maintaining parallel static-PDF processes—is genuinely resource-efficient and leverages infrastructure we already run, which aligns well with my mandate to stretch limited implementation capacity. The core idea—automating extraction of technical documentation from artifacts we already produce (code repos, experiment logs, commit histories)—is genuinely resource-efficient at scale: it amortizes a recurring compliance cost across every future high-risk system and leverages existing R&D infrastructure without adding new data-collection overhead. However, framing this as a 'research challenge' that requires building novel LLM-based agents invites scope creep and opportunity-cost risk; the engineers pulled off active R&D projects to build a custom documentation pipeline could instead be applying off-the-shelf LLM APIs against structured templates in a fraction of the time, achieving 80% of the compliance benefit at a much lower draw on scarce implementation bandwidth. The pilot-first scoping is prudent, but as written this commits real engineering capacity to an R&D deliverable when the obligation it serves is fundamentally operational.

This is a textbook resource-allocation play: one centralized engineering build replaces N per-project logging implementations, directly protecting scarce systems-engineering headcount so it can remain directed at research rather than compliance plumbing. The explicit commitment to integrate with *existing* training pipelines (rather than mandating a rip-and-replace) also means we respect sunk infrastructure investment and avoid the capital outlay that would strain our funding envelope.

Decoupling Article 12 logging into a service-mesh sidecar amortises the one-time infrastructure investment across all current and future high-risk deployments, eliminating the per-project tax on researchers' time and reducing the risk of compliance gaps from inconsistent manual instrumentation. The main caveat is that network-level capture handles transport events (timestamps, payloads) well but will not by itself yield every semantic field mandated by Article 12(3) for Annex III 1(a) systems—reference-database provenance and verifier identity still need thin application-level hooks—so the lab should budget a modest residual layer of per-deployment annotation on top of the mesh rather than treating this as a complete solution.

This is a well-scoped, bounded engineering investment that plugs directly into infrastructure we already run (CI/CD pipelines, version control) to eliminate a recurring administrative bottleneck across every build and future system; the upfront scripting cost is finite and recovers quickly once multiple high-risk models cycle through deployment. The main residual risk from my vantage point is that purely metadata-driven generation may not capture all narrative elements of the EU AI Act template (risk-management rationale, stated limitations), so some human-authored sections will remain — but automating 70-80% of the repetitive fields is a substantial resource-efficiency gain without diverting funding from active research.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, this is well-scoped: event-triggered report generation (on model update or test) piggybacks on cycles we already run rather than imposing continuous monitoring overhead, and dataset version control plus automated doc generation are natural extensions of MLOps tooling most serious labs have already deployed. The secondary benefit—reproducibility records that also serve scientific debugging and drift analysis—means the compliance spend is not pure regulatory tax but doubles as infrastructure we would want anyway; however, the 'real-time' framing in the title risks pulling engineering resources toward unnecessary streaming architecture if not explicitly bounded to event-driven batch triggers at our existing model-update cadence.

Article 12's logging obligations are met with standard software-engineering work (structured event pipelines, pseudonymized data retention, access controls); the GDPR tension it cites is largely resolvable through existing anonymisation/pseudonymisation practice without frontier cryptography. Committing scarce R&D headcount to ZKP/SMPC research—areas where I lack in-house cryptographer depth and specialised compute infrastructure—while the actual compliance requirement is a well-understood engineering task, misallocates resources and introduces execution risk (including the open question whether a regulator accepts cryptographic commitments as 'logs' under Recital 71's comprehensibility expectation).

This proposal is well-scoped for resource efficiency: it hooks into PyTorch pipelines the lab already runs, so the marginal cost is metadata instrumentation rather than a new platform, and it delivers dual value (regulatory traceability plus reproducibility) from a single engineering investment. My only reservation is that its emphasis on training-cycle provenance addresses Recital 71's technical-documentation requirements but does not by itself cover Article 12(3)'s operational-deployment logging mandates (per-use timestamps, reference-database pointers, verification-personnel IDs), so it is a strong foundation rather than full compliance; still, as an increment built on existing infrastructure with no new headcount line, it clears my bar comfortably.

This is a pragmatic compliance-automation play that slots naturally onto experiment-tracking infrastructure we already maintain (MLflow/W&B/DVC-style pipelines), so the marginal build cost is primarily a templating and export layer rather than a new data-capture system. The core value proposition—decoupling dossier assembly from research velocity—is exactly the efficiency lever I care about, since having senior researchers hand-assemble Recital 71 documentation at every model milestone is a poor use of scarce senior time. My main reservation is scope ambiguity: 'EU-compliant technical documentation' as envisioned by Recital 71 reaches well beyond hyperparameters and dataset versions into risk-management narrative, capability/limitation characterisation, and algorithmic-process documentation that no template engine can fully auto-generate, so the proposal risks underestimating ongoing maintenance as implementing acts mature. Still, committing moderate engineering effort now to automate the structured-data portion (lineage, versioning, validation artifacts) is a clearly justified use of existing infrastructure against a mandatory obligation, and it frees researcher-hours for actual R&D.

This is precisely the resource-allocation discipline my function exists to enforce: a lightweight, periodic governance step (leadership reviewing charters against Annex III) that prevents both the over-provisioning of compute and storage on non-high-risk projects and the reactive scramble for infrastructure when a project crosses into high-risk territory. As a process change rather than an engineering build, it has low implementation cost relative to the misallocation risk it eliminates, which is exactly the efficiency calculus I am accountable for.

From a resource-allocation standpoint this is squarely on-target: it replaces N parallel, bespoke logging implementations (one per research team) with a single shared engineering artifact that maps directly onto the minimum fields in Art. 12(3) (timestamps, reference database, input data match, verifying-person ID), so every high-risk project inherits compliance plumbing without consuming its own headcount on it. The modular-API framing also protects scientific ambition by keeping domain scientists out of low-level traceability code and letting them focus compute cycles and model-development effort where the lab's competitive advantage actually lies; the main residual risk is scoping — if 'modular' turns into a rigid monolith that can't accommodate project-specific event schemas beyond the statutory minimum, we'll end up forking it per-team anyway and the efficiency gain evaporates.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, centralising compliance logging into a single WORM object-store layer is exactly the right infrastructure bet: it converts what would otherwise be per-project storage engineering (duplicative, expensive in engineer-hours) into one shared, low-marginal-cost service that scales across all current and future high-risk systems. Cloud-native object storage with object-lock is mature commodity infrastructure—not an R&D gamble—so the lab spends a bounded setup cost to satisfy Article 12(1)–(3) without diverting scarce compute or engineering capacity away from actual scientific work, while the 'write-once' semantics directly guarantee the lifetime log persistence and audit-integrity that regulators will test.

This proposal extracts scientific output from an obligation we are already bearing: Article 12(1) mandates that our high-risk systems produce lifetime logs regardless of whether we study them, so the data-collection cost is effectively sunk. The analytical work (time-series anomaly detection on event streams) can be absorbed by existing statistical tooling and analyst capacity without new hardware or headcount, making it one of the higher value-per-marginal-resource proposals in the batch; my only reservation is that 'advanced' and open-ended 'research project' language risk scope creep unless the engagement is bounded to a defined analytical sprint against a specific deployed system cohort.

The core direction—automating compliance logging to free researcher time and satisfy Article 12(1)–(3)—is well-aligned with our efficiency mandate, since the scarcest resource in this lab is senior research expertise, not disk I/O. From a resource-allocation standpoint, building one shared logging library that amortizes the Article 12(1) compliance cost across all high-risk projects is far more efficient than letting each team bolt on its own ad-hoc logger; it directly cuts per-project implementation overhead and frees researcher hours for model work rather than compliance plumbing. The scope—API hooks plus default capture of timestamps, input hashes, and user identifiers—is tightly bounded to what the regulation mandates (and partially anticipates the Annex III 1(a) specifics in Art. 12(3)), making it a well-proportioned infrastructure investment that leverages our existing multi-project structure without requiring a platform rebuild.

Article 12 mandates automatic event logging and specific data fields for traceability — a bounded engineering task — but this proposal layers on an open-ended research project (specialized LLM development, a novel failure-mode taxonomy) that the regulation does not require. The strategic logic is sound from a resource-allocation standpoint: gating full Article 12 instrumentation to the production-promotion point avoids burning scarce engineering and compute cycles on exploratory work that may never reach high-risk status, while the 'wrapper' framing lets us leverage existing prototype infrastructure rather than rebuilding our R&D stack. The main reservation is that building a dedicated mirrored execution environment plus a compliance-container layer represents meaningful upfront capital before any single system actually triggers the obligation, and the proposal doesn't clearly scope which projects flow through this gate versus those that remain in indefinite research — a scoping gap that could inflate cost if applied indiscriminately.

The underlying compliance need (storing Article 12(3) fields with tamper-evidence for Annex III §1(a) systems) is genuine and mandatory, but the proposal as framed commits scarce resources to a greenfield 'dedicated' storage layer—and prominently toils toward a distributed ledger—when our existing logging pipelines, model-versioning stores (MLflow/DVC), and dataset registries can be extended with append-only hash-chaining and retention policies at a fraction of the build cost. From an infrastructure-leverage standpoint, this duplicates capability we already own and over-engineers relative to what Article 12(3) actually requires (four structured data points per event, retained for system lifetime).

This is a high-leverage efficiency play that directly addresses an ongoing, compounding cost: the manual labor of keeping technical documentation current throughout a system's lifetime (a Recital 71 obligation). The core concept—centralising compliance logging into a single reusable module—is directionally sound for resource efficiency (build once, deploy many), but the proposal as scoped commits engineering capacity to a mandatory wrapper across *all* R&D projects rather than only those pipelines that will actually produce high-risk systems under Article 12, and it proposes net-new infrastructure without first assessing whether our existing telemetry, run-tracking, and experiment-logging frameworks already capture most of the required fields (timestamps, dataset provenance, operator IDs). In a lab where pipeline architectures are deliberately heterogeneous to support experimentation, a single mandatory API wrapper risks creating a high-friction integration bottleneck that diverts senior engineers from scientific work for marginal compliance gain on projects that will never ship as high-risk systems.

From a resource-allocation standpoint, centralising a mandatory Article 12 obligation into a single reusable middleware layer is textbook efficiency: one build cost amortised across every high-risk project, no duplicated per-team logging code, and it slots naturally onto monitoring infrastructure we already operate. Still, the strategic direction—build once, deploy everywhere, let researchers stay on science while compliance is handled at the platform tier—is exactly the kind of leverage a well-run lab should be extracting from its existing infrastructure.

The proposal addresses a real engineering concern—logging overhead at scale—but the techniques it proposes (differentially private sketching, approximate compressed event streams) are fundamentally incompatible with Article 12(3)'s requirement for exact, individually identifiable records (specific start/end timestamps, precise input data matches, named natural persons). Allocating dedicated research resources to explore novel algorithmic approaches when the compliance bar is a bounded set of structured fields best served by well-understood append-only logging and standard compression represents poor resource-allocation efficiency; the 'significant scientific contribution' framing overstates what is effectively an incremental engineering optimization that existing infrastructure teams can handle without a new R&D project.

This proposal speaks directly to my core mandate: it converts an open-ended regulatory obligation into a bounded, predictable line-item within existing project budgets, which is the single most efficient way to absorb Article 12's logging requirements without derailing scientific timelines or triggering catastrophic late-stage redesigns (the costliest failure mode in any R&D lab). This proposal is a textbook case of extracting regulatory compliance value from infrastructure we already operate—experiment trackers, VCS metadata, and training logs are generated as byproducts of normal R&D work, so the incremental resource cost is essentially an engineering transformation layer rather than a new data-collection or research programme. This proposal directly addresses my core mandate: it eliminates duplicated logging-engineering effort across every high-risk project by centralizing a single shared module, explicitly leverages our existing compute clusters rather than requiring new procurement, and—critically—frees researchers from writing boilerplate compliance code so their time stays on actual science.
